newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST - AIB 1996 profits to rise by 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - AIB 1996 profits to rise by 10 pct.

text.p: Ireland's largest bank, Allied Irish Banks Plc, is expected to announce an increase of over 10 percent in 1996 pre-tax profits when it releases full-year results next Tuesday, analysts said.

Buoyed by the strong economic climate in Ireland, a better-than-expected performance from its U.S. operations and the 1995 acquisition of John Govett, the bank is expected to report pre-tax profits of 412.5 to 413.0 million Irish pounds ($659-660 million) compared with 372.6 million in 1995, analysts said.
Earnings per share of 37.4-37.5 pence are expected while the bank is seen paying a dividend of 14.7 to 15 pence per share.

Goodbody Stockbrokers expects AIB Bank, the retail division which has operations in the Republic of Ireland, Northern Ireland and Britain, to contribute pre-tax profits of 212 million to a total of 412.5 million.
Analysts say that the bank could even surprise on the upside as credit growth at the licensed banks in Ireland was stronger than expected in the second half of 1996.

Figures released on Thursday showed that the adjusted annual rate of private sector credit growth in Ireland was 14.9 percent at end-December after 16.5 percent in November and 14.4 percent in October.
New business figures already released by AIB's life assurance unit, Ark Life, also bode well, analysts say.
Ark Life reported that new regular premium sales rose by 84 percent in 1996 while single premium sales were up 57 percent.
Meanwhile, AIB's U.S. subsidiary, First Maryland Bancorp, reported a 10 percent increase in 1996 net income to $132.34 million in January, ahead of market forecasts.
Goodbody analyst Oliver O'Shea estimates that the U.S. division, which also includes AIB's New York office, should contribute 116 million punts to profits.
"The news we have heard so far has been positive," he said.

Analysts say the capital markets division should benefit from the acquisition in December 1995 of UK fund manager John Govett and is expected to turn in profits of 71 million Irish pounds against 58 million last year.
The results, if they come in on target, should lend support to the share price which has gained around nine percent since AIB said it was buying U.S. bank Dauphin Deposit Corp, analysts said.
AIB announced on January 21 that it was buying the Pennsylvania bank for $1.36 billion, the biggest takeover in Irish corporate history.
